lesson.title: From Sandbox to Street: Running a Real Pilot
lesson.summary: A pilot moves beyond a proof of concept's narrow technical test into real users, real data, and production-like conditions within a deliberately limited scope, guided by success and exit criteria fixed before it begins.
lesson.body:
A proof of concept answers a narrow technical question in a controlled sandbox. A pilot program is the next, much bigger step: running the system with real users, real or realistic data, and production-like operating conditions, but within a deliberately limited scope, a single business unit, a single geography, a single product line, a fixed set of consortium partners, so that the organization can learn what actually happens at meaningful scale before committing to full production and everything that entails.

Because a pilot is where the organizational challenges chapter's concerns finally become visible in practice, its design has to account for them directly. Real consortium members have to actually agree to the governance terms discussed earlier in this course, not just in principle but in a signed operating arrangement covering the pilot's specific scope. Real stakeholder buy-in has to hold up under real friction, not just survive a slide deck. Real integration with legacy systems has to actually work, including the failure modes and edge cases that a synthetic PoC dataset never exercises. A pilot that succeeds only because it was run by the most enthusiastic, most technically capable team in the organization, under conditions unusually favorable compared to a full rollout, has told you less than it appears to.

The discipline that separates a useful pilot from an open-ended, drifting one is defining both success criteria and exit criteria before the pilot starts, and this is where the change management chapter's warning about sunk cost and loss aversion becomes directly actionable. Success criteria specify, in measurable terms, what result justifies scaling to full production: a defined reduction in dispute resolution time, a defined transaction volume sustained reliably, a defined level of participant satisfaction. Exit criteria specify, just as concretely, what result justifies stopping the project rather than continuing to invest in it, and fixing those criteria in advance, while the team is still reasoning from evidence rather than from months of accumulated investment, is what keeps a struggling pilot from being extended indefinitely purely because stopping it would feel like admitting the earlier investment was wasted.

A concrete example makes the shape clear. A consortium of three real supplier partners agrees to track a single product line's provenance on a shared ledger for ninety days, using real shipments rather than test data, with the explicit success criterion that discrepancy investigations must drop by a defined margin compared to the partners' historical baseline, and the explicit exit criterion that persistent integration failures with any partner's existing systems, unresolved after a defined remediation window, will end the pilot rather than trigger an open-ended extension. At the end of the ninety days, the decision to scale, extend, or stop is made against those pre-committed numbers, not against how invested everyone has become in the meantime. That discipline, not the ledger's cryptography, is usually what determines whether a pilot becomes a production system or a well-intentioned dead end.
